# Farrah Fawcett's Battle with Cancer: A Friend's Reflections

*(CNN)* — Farrah Fawcett, the actress celebrated worldwide for her beauty and her iconic role on "Charlie's Angels," is reportedly gravely ill and may be nearing the end of a prolonged struggle with cancer. Fawcett, pictured here in 2004, is the subject of a documentary chronicling her courageous fight against the disease.

The documentary, set to air Friday night on NBC, offers an intimate portrait of her life since receiving her diagnosis. On Thursday, Larry King spoke with Candy Spelling, a longtime friend of Fawcett's whose late husband, Aaron Spelling, produced "Charlie's Angels." In the conversation, Spelling reflects on her enduring friendship with Fawcett and shares her thoughts on why Fawcett chose to participate in the documentary. Below is an edited transcript of their discussion.

**Larry King:** Did you first meet Farrah in connection with her landing that role?

**Candy Spelling:** Yes. She actually took on several small parts in projects Aaron was producing, beginning around 1973. So it's been—my goodness—thirty-six or thirty-seven years since I first met her.

*Watch Candy Spelling discuss her friendship with Farrah Fawcett »*

**King:** So you've known her well throughout all these years?

**Spelling:** Yes.

**King:** Were you aware when she was cast in "Charlie's Angels"?

**Spelling:** I recall she had taken on a few minor roles beforehand. I believe the project that convinced Aaron of her potential was one centered on a beauty pageant, along with "Murder on Flight 502"—one of the ninety-minute television films he produced.

**King:** A movie of the week?

**Spelling:** That's right. Movies of the week.

**King:** When did you learn she had cancer?

**Spelling:** I found out roughly a year—or perhaps two—ago, when the news first reached me. I reached out to her, having not spoken with her in some time. She told me, "I'm going to be all right, Candy. Everything is going to be all right."

**King:** Why do you believe she chose to do the documentary, Candy?

**Spelling:** I believe she wanted to inspire courage in others facing similar battles. I witnessed firsthand how devastating media scrutiny was for Aaron during his own struggle with cancer—it's an incredibly difficult experience. Maintaining any sense of privacy under such circumstances becomes nearly impossible.

**King:** Why does the tabloid press become so relentless toward someone enduring such suffering?

**Spelling:** It sells. It's truly unfortunate, and I always feel for those caught in it. But people tend to believe what they read, even though we often can't be certain how accurate it truly is.
